q: I have drawn Isa. How does it come into this?
text: Isa comes into the crossing as the winter you were born in. The two arms still meet, but for now nothing moves between them — the giving hand and the cupped one both keep their place, and the water in the bowl stands level because the carrying has stopped. The fire is not out; it is banked, the way the land held its breath at Jól. What Isa stills is not the balance. It is the passing itself, for as long as the cold lasts.

q: I have drawn Jera. How does it come into this?
text: Jera comes into the crossing as the season it was set in. You came at Jól, on the year's darkest hinge — and Jera is that hinge still turning: the light coming back at its own pace, not at yours. What passes between the two arms now passes slowly, the way a banked fire keeps its heat for morning. Nothing at the middle is asked to hurry. What crosses there has a calendar of its own, older than the one on the wall.

q: I have drawn Perth. How does it come into this?
text: Perth comes into the crossing as the wrapped gift. One of the two arms reaches out of somewhere you cannot see — something is already travelling toward the middle, and what it is will only be known when it arrives and the hand opens. Your palm is used to knowing what it gives. This time the not-knowing sits at the centre of the crossing, held like the rún your name keeps: carried between two, read by neither, until its hour.

q: I have drawn Gebo — my own rune. How does it come into this?
text: Gebo falls into Gebo the way a path crosses its own track — you have come to this middle before, from the other side. The crossing in you is now also the crossing in front of you: the same open palm, met this time by another open palm, and for once neither of them is yours. What the rune asks doubled is what it asked single, only louder — the cupped hand, the gift let in. The balance in the bowl tips toward receiving.
